The addition of NH4I turned precipitate yellow. That suggests formation of PbI2 (yellow). So Pb2+ is present. Good.

Now we need to see if Ag+ or Hg2+ also present. The initial white precipitate could be mixture of AgCl and PbCl2 etc. Since we have Pb2+, we need to test for Ag+ and Hg2+.

We can test filtrate after HCl precipitation (g1mix4_filtrate) for presence of Ag+ or Hg2+ using appropriate reagents: Add NH4SCN to detect Ag+ (forms white precipitate of AgSCN) or add DMG for Ni? Not.

Better: Use addition of NaCl? Already have chloride.

To test for Ag+, we can add dilute NH3 to filtrate; if Ag+ present, will precipitate AgCl? Actually Ag+ already would have precipitated as AgCl with HCl, so if Ag+ present, it would be in precipitate, not filtrate. So we need to test precipitate for Ag+. Use addition of NH3 to precipitate: AgCl dissolves, forming colorless solution. Our precipitate turned yellow with I- (PbI2). That suggests Pb2+ present. To see if AgCl also present, we can add excess NH3 to precipitate and see if any dissolution (clear solution). In our precipitate test with NH3 earlier, precipitate turned gray, not dissolved. That suggests no AgCl. For Hg2+, we can add KI? Mercurous iodide is white? Not.

We can test with H2S in acidic medium: Add H2S(acidic) to filtrate (which contains any remaining cations that didn't precipitate with HCl). If Ag+ or Hg2+ present, they would have precipitated already, so filtrate likely contains other cations (maybe not group I). But we need to confirm absence of Ag+ and Hg2+. Could test with addition of NH4SCN to filtrate; Ag+ forms white precipitate of AgSCN, Hg2+ forms? Not.
